stories.headline: 'Under Kolkata Police watch': Abhishek Banerjee alleges midnight BJP attack on home
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Trinamool Congress
 (TMC) National General Secretary 
Abhishek Banerjee
 on Saturday alleged that his residence was attacked by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) workers around 2 am on Saturday, accusing the Kolkata Police of failing to prevent the incident.
In a post on social media platform X, Banerjee claimed that the alleged attack took place shortly after he released a video showing unidentified individuals conducting reconnaissance of his office and residence.
"After I released the recce video this morning, my house was attacked just now, at 2 AM by BJP goons, right under the watch of the Kolkata police," he said.
The TMC leader also criticised the Calcutta High Court and the Supreme Court over their alleged inaction, saying, "Thank you, Calcutta High Court and the Supreme Court of India, for remaining mute spectators while all this unfolds. I will upload the videos shortly."
Earlier on Friday, Banerjee had alleged that unidentified individuals had been conducting surveillance of his office and residence for the past two days. He claimed that when confronted, the individuals identified themselves as police personnel.
"For the past two days, a few unidentified individuals have been conducting reconnaissance of my office and residence. The registration number of their motorcycle is mentioned below. 
When confronted, they claimed to be police personnel," he said.
Questioning the alleged surveillance, Banerjee asked why the state police were monitoring the premises of an elected Member of Parliament and who had authorised the operation.

"Why is the State Police allegedly spying on and snooping around the office and residence of an elected Member of Parliament? Who authorised this surveillance and for what purpose?" he asked.
Describing the matter as a suspected conspiracy, the TMC leader demanded an immediate and thorough investigation to establish the identities of those involved, identify who had directed the alleged surveillance and determine its purpose.
"I am immediately drawing the attention of the Hon’ble Speaker of the Lok Sabha @ombirlakota, @kolkata_police, @HMOIndia @WBPolice to this extremely serious matter. I demand an immediate and thorough inquiry to establish the identity of these individuals, who sent them and to uncover the nefarious motive behind this suspected conspiracy," he said.

stories.headline: ‘Legends don't say goodbye’: Ex-cricketer's tribute for Shami after retirement
stories.deck: Mohammed Shami has officially announced his retirement from Test cricket, marking the end of a distinguished twelve-year journey. Over his career, he participated in 64 Tests, claiming 229 wickets for India, with standout performances particularly against South Africa and Australia. Manoj Tiwary, his fellow cricketer, honored Shami's impact on the sport, calling him a true warrior. Shami plans to…
stories.bodyText:
Former India cricketer and ex-Bengal captain 
Manoj Tiwary
 paid an emotional tribute to 
Mohammed Shami
 after the veteran fast bowler announced his retirement from Test cricket on Friday, bringing the curtain down on a 12-year career in the longest format.
Tiwary, who had the opportunity to lead Bengal with 
Shami
 in his bowling attack, took to X to reflect on the pacer's impact and recall his association with the speedster. He described Shami as a warrior, while also highlighting the lasting memories he had created through his performances in the red-ball format.
"The red ball may no longer be in his hands, but the memories of his thunderbolts will forever remain in the hearts of cricket lovers. Some legends don't say goodbye; they simply become history," Tiwary wrote.
Recalling his time as Bengal captain, he added: "This what it meant to me When I was leading the bengal team and having Shami in the bowling line up. Warrior at heart"
Shami's announcement brings an end to an impressive Test career spanning 64 matches, during which he picked up 229 wickets. The 36-year-old made the announcement through an Instagram post, confirming that while he would no longer represent India in the white jersey, he intended to continue playing white-ball cricket.
"I am leaving the white jersey, but never the memories connected to it. When I first wore India's Test jersey, I had only a dream — to do something for my country. After that every wicket, every struggle, every injury and every comeback taught me something," Shami wrote.
"Test cricket is not just a format for me, it is a very special part of my life. Today I am deciding to retire from Test cricket with a heavy heart and unlimited beautiful memories," he added.
A 12-year journey in India's Test colours
Shami made his Test debut against the West Indies at Kolkata's Eden Gardens on November 6, 2013. He ended his career with 229 wickets at an average of 27.71, including six five-wicket hauls.
His ability to extract movement through seam and swing with both the new and old ball made him a crucial member of India's pace attack across different conditions.
Of his 229 wickets, 131 came in 35 Tests played in South Africa, the West Indies and India, where he maintained an average of under 25.
South Africa witnessed some of Shami's finest performances in Test cricket. During India's 2018 tour, he produced a match-winning spell of 5/28 in the second innings of the Johannesburg Test, helping the visitors secure a consolation victory.
On India's subsequent visit to the country, he continued his impressive record by claiming eight wickets in the series-opening Test at Centurion.
Shami's final appearance in Test cricket came in the 2023 World Test Championship final against Australia at Lord's. Injuries later disrupted his career, and he remained out of the Indian team after the 2025 Champions Trophy, before deciding to bring his red-ball journey to a close.

stories.headline: ‘I’d always disliked politics’ | An excerpt from Sonia Gandhi’s ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’
stories.deck: In her memoir, the senior Congress party leader revisits the years of hesitation and personal conflict before duty finally prevailed
stories.bodyText:
With Rajiv gone, everything around me echoed and re-echoed my loss. While I found some solace in the tasks centred on his memory, I was confronted with my fragility whenever the need arose to make public appearances. They couldn’t be avoided: there was the work of various memorial trusts that I headed, which had to continue — international conferences and lectures. At such functions I was required to welcome the guests with a speech. I would have to wrestle with my agitation in the preceding days and the fear that tears would overwhelm me suddenly while I was addressing the audience. That would happen also when visitors condoled with me. I remember when His Holiness the Dalai Lama came and asked me in his usual matter-of-fact manner, “Do you feel vengeful towards those who killed Rajiv?” I replied, “No, I don’t,” and burst into sobs.
That vulnerability remained with me for a long time, but slowly, slowly, the days began to feel less empty and endless. Sleep returned. Rajiv became a presence within me rather than a piercing absence in my life, though the anguish returned in force every time we — Rahul and Priyanka as well as I — shared something important, a rite of passage in which he would have been a vital participant — like their graduations, his daughter’s wedding, later the birth of his grandchildren.
Priyanka graduated with a degree in psychology in 1993 from Jesus and Mary College. Rahul graduated with a master of philosophy (M.Phil) degree from Trinity College in 1995. Priyanka and I decided to attend his convocation, and my mother and younger sister joined us with two of my nieces. Rahul could barely contain his happiness when we turned up; beaming from ear to ear, he embraced all six of us.
To be walking again the narrow streets of Cambridge, still thriving and thrumming with students, passing by old haunts — the Varsity restaurant, my old language school, Rajiv’s lodgings on Kimberley Road and mine on Tenison Road — brought back memories of when he and I first met, of our blissful time together. During the moving graduation ceremony in the Senate House, as Rahul received his degree, I struggled to suppress my tears. Rahul and Priyanka were similarly overcome. How they missed their father at that special moment, how proud Rajiv would have felt of his son.
* * *
Time flowed on. As I gradually emerged from seclusion and became a little more active, once in a while Rajiv’s former colleagues would visit — some for a courtesy call, or to invite me to a family function, others with pleas that I take an active interest in party affairs. To the latter I would listen quietly but not heed their request.
The 1996 election results were disappointing for the Congress Party. It had not been able to form a government on its own. It was plagued by splits and factional disputes. In 1995 I had been asked to support one particular group, in which the main actors were Arjun Singh, N.D. Tiwari, and Mohsina Kidwai, who’d been party members for decades and had held important positions and ministries. I had refused. They broke away and formed another party, followed the next year by senior Tamil leaders G.K. Moopanar and P. Chidambaram, and a younger Congress member, Madhavrao Scindia, who’d joined in 1980. All of them set up separate parties. In 1997 Mamata Banerjee left, due to differences with the state leadership, and formed her own party, the Trinamool Congress. I had become a primary member in 1997 when I was invited by the Congress President Sitaram Kesri to the party’s 80th Plenary Session in Calcutta, but as the party’s situation seemed to be worsening, the pressure on me was increasing to take over its leadership.
I began to feel agitated, brooding on what was going on in the Congress Party, worrying about its fate. Articles in the media were painting a sorry picture of its future. Each time I walked past Rajiv’s picture and my mother-in-law’s, a mixture of pain and guilt would seize me; at times I’d even deliberately avoid looking at them. The India of my belonging had come to me through my husband and my mother-in-law. The very forces they had fought against for decades to protect India’s pluralistic ethos were now bent upon a path that would do untold damage. How could I sit comfortably at home and let their work and their sacrifices go in vain?
I felt tormented. I’d wake up in the middle of the night wondering what I should do, asking myself which way I should go. Had I not fought at every step against a life in politics? Had it not cruelly taken away from me first my mother-in-law, then the love of my life, my children’s father? Why, why was I feeling that strong urge to respond to the demand being made of me? I’d always disliked politics, even during all the years when Rajiv was in public life. But now I was beginning to understand what had compelled him, what I had then so strongly resisted: the pull of duty towards his mother, his country. That pull was now getting hold of me. It scared me, I tried to fight it, but it kept coming back to haunt me.
I was caught in a war with myself: part of me recoiled at the world of politics, of the ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery that goes inescapably with the game of power everywhere. But I couldn’t repudiate the inner compulsions that had been drilled into me from my childhood — diligence in assigned tasks, respect towards elders, obedience to parents, fidelity to family norms. They kept gnawing at me. Where my duty lay was clear to me; what that implied was the terrifying part.
I’d seen that world. I had experienced it through Rajiv: in its peaks of high endeavour and achievement, as well as in all its ugliness and venality. How could I even think of getting into it? And to lead the party in an impending electoral battle? Where was my experience, where was my ability or understanding of the task — a task that had often frustrated even the tallest leaders of the past? I was after all the outsider. I had been reminded of that status again and again. Yes, I was Indira Gandhi’s daughter-in-law, Rajiv Gandhi’s widow — but how dare I even think of stepping into a party position they had occupied, I asked myself.
I had no right — except for the fact that I carried the family name: a name that had a wide appeal across the country because it signified devoted service and allegiance to the all inclusive ethos of India, above and beyond categories of religion, caste, language, or region. It was for that reason that so many Congress men and women were pleading with me to come forward to head the party; otherwise, it would break up and scatter — as it was now doing. Soon there would be nothing left to hold back the relentless advance of the communal forces, they urged. And that was for me the most compelling argument.
The struggle went on, through nights of broken sleep and anxious days. I felt tortured, alone — longing for something, an anchor to hold on to, someone, something to guide me and help me out of my fears and doubts. Was it a subconscious search that would lead me to where I already knew in my heart I had to go?
I’ve never been religious in all my adult life, though I respect all faiths, but it was during this period that I felt the urge to go back to the Bhagavad Gita. I had read it when I was much younger. The ancient book and the great story of which it was a part were everywhere, permeating the life and thought of millions. I was aware of its profound effect on the heroes of the independence movement. I’d witnessed its representations in theatre, in festivals and other forms. I’d heard its couplets recited again and again by political personalities to make a point or to enlighten.
I knew of the Lal Bahadur Shastri Sanskrit Vidyapeeth. Careful not to disclose the reason for my request, I asked my office to enquire if I could take some classes at home. The name of Professor Vachaspati Upadhyaya — “Shastriji” as we called him, a gentle, unassuming, and erudite scholar who was also known to our family — came up. He kindly agreed to explain the deeper philosophical meaning of the Gita to me in his spare time.
Starting in January 1997, I sat with him periodically over a volume chosen from Rajiv’s bookshelves, a Sanskrit edition with Hindi and English translations below each couplet. Shastriji would recite a verse or two in Sanskrit, I’d read out the Hindi translation, and he’d explain the meaning. We started slowly, but I see from my office appointment diary that in December 1997 we had many sessions. Our readings continued at a pace until our last one, on January 5, 1998.
Rahul and Priyanka were aware of my restlessness and feared I might allow myself to get drawn into politics. Just as I had fought with Rajiv, my two children now argued fiercely with me. They had been through the ordeals of losing their grandmother and their father; there were only the three of us now left of our family; they didn’t want to lose me, too, they said emphatically. They extracted a promise from me before leaving for their New Year vacation: “Happy New Year, Mama. Don’t you do anything crazy while we’re away. You’ve promised us, remember.”
I was on my own now with my churning thoughts. The readings were drawing to a close. Krishna has expounded the message of the Gita: Perform your dharma without regard for the fruit of your action. Arjuna, the Pandava prince, declares that his illusion is now dispelled; he is restored to himself, firm and free from all doubts, and ready to play his part in the battle.
Something awoke in me: I was sure. I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did.
Excerpted from ‘Belonging: A Journey of Love’ (HarperCollins India).

stories.headline: Google executive Donald Harrison resigns from SpaceX board
stories.bodyText: SpaceX disclosed on Friday that Google executive Donald Harrison has resigned from the rockets-to-AI company's board after more than a decade. Here are some details Harrison notified SpaceX of his resignation on November 4, and it took effect immediately The Elon Musk-led company said Harrison's decision to resign was not due to any disagreement with the company on matters relating to its operations, policies or practices Harrison, a longtime executive at Google, is currently president of Global Partnerships and Corporate Development. Google parent Alphabet is the largest single institutional holder of SpaceX, according to LSEG data Musk said that Harrison stepped down because there were too many conflicts of interest with Alphabet. briefs.headline: Explosion at police outpost in Ghaziabad’s Vasundhara; 1 injured
briefs.deck: An explosion occurred at the Vasundhara police outpost in Ghaziabad, resulting in injuries to a delivery worker. The delivery boy was present at the police post when the blast happened and was hurt by glass shards. Authorities have confirmed that a sub-inspector was also on-site during the explosion. Police are now conducting an investigation to determine the cause of the incident.
briefs.bodyText:
GHAZIABAD: An explosion was reported at a police outpost in Uttar Pradesh's Ghaziabad district, leaving a delivery worker injured after shattered glass hit him.
According to news agency ANI, the incident took place at the Vasundhara police chowki, which falls under the jurisdiction of Indirapuram police station.
According to Indirapuram ACP Suryabali Maurya, a sub-inspector and a delivery boy were present at the outpost when the explosion occurred.
The delivery worker had arrived to deliver an item and sustained injuries from the shattered glass.
"The exact nature of the object that caused the explosion will only be determined following an investigation. A sub-inspector from the Vasundhara police outpost and a delivery boy, who had arrived to drop off an item, were present at the scene. The delivery boy sustained injuries from the shattered glass," Maurya said.
Further details are awaited.

briefs.headline: Calcutta High Court restrains KMC polls until challenge on delimitation decided
briefs.deck: The West Bengal government, through a delimitation, has increased the number of wards of KMC from 144 to 209. The petitioner argued that the State government and its agencies have resorted to gerrymandering in order to secure partisan advantage to the ruling political party in West Bengal on the premise of previous electoral results.
briefs.bodyText:
The Calcutta High Court on Friday (October 6, 2026) restrained the West Bengal State Election Commission from issuing any notification for the upcoming Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections based on newly redrawn wards until a pending petition challenging the delimitation exercise is decided.
The West Bengal government had passed a legislation in the State Assembly on August 12, redrawing the wards of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and increasing the number of wards from 144 to 209. Dipu Das, a former councillor of the city’s civic body had challenged the delimitation exercise before the Calcutta High Court.
“Accordingly, MAT No.1917 of 2026 is allowed on contest, thereby modifying the impugned Order dated October 29, 2026 passed in WPA No.31433 of 2026 by restraining the respondent no. 6, that is, the West Bengal State Election Commission, from issuing any notification calling an election to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation on the basis of the amended Schedule II of the KMC Act as notified in the Official Gazette vide Notification No.1728/UDMA-15011(22)/57/2026-LS-MA SEC dated September 11, 2026 till disposal of WPA No.31433 of 2026,” an order by the Division Bench of Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Arjun Ray Mukherjee.
The appeal by the petitioner challenged an October 29 order by Justice Hiranmay Bhattacharyya, who had refused to stay the State government’s delimitation notification proposing amendments to Schedule II of the KMC Act.
The development casts uncertainty over holding of the elections to KMC, something that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government was keen on. In fact, the BJP leadership had started the process of selecting candidates. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has on several occasions, expressed their preference to hold civic body elections in Kolkata and Howrah by the end of November or early December this year.
After the BJP came to power in May 2026, the KMC board, led by former Mayor Firhad Hakim, and the councillors resigned, and the State government appointed administrators to run West Bengal’s largest civic body.
Appearing for the petitioner, senior advocate Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya questioned whether the administrator, appointed by the State Government upon dissolution of the corporation, could act as the “Corporation” and issue such a recommendation to reorganise the boards.
Mr. Bhattacharya said that the State Government and its agencies have resorted to gerrymandering in order to secure a partisan advantage for the ruling political party in West Bengal on the premise of previous electoral results, without considering relevant circumstances such as geographical contiguity, compactness and administrative convenience, involving huge expenses from the public exchequer.
Advocate General S.N. Mitra argued that, under Section 601 of the KMC Act, the State Government itself has ample power to add, alter, or modify the Schedules of the KMC Act, irrespective of whether any recommendation is made by the Corporation or not and thus, the appellant’s contentions in that regard were irrelevant.
The Court, however, held the writ petitioner has made out a sufficiently strong prima facie case in the writ petition to be favoured with interim protection in order to save the writ petition from being rendered in-fructuous.

briefs.headline: How a love story grew into a deep belonging to India
briefs.deck: Sonia Gandhi’s much-awaited Belonging is a personal memoir, with politics providing the background or “a kind of framework,” as she puts it in the book
briefs.bodyText:
In an interview to The HinduBelonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi observed that under the Bharatiya Janata Party-Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh dispensation over the last twelve years, “great damage has been done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions. Even after this government goes, it will take time to restore our systems back to health, and great effort from political parties. People are now beginning to be restless and recognising the damage. But I am optimistic and I know that the people of India will welcome a return to proper governance.”
Asked about the decline of the Congress as India’s dominant party, the view of some critics that the party has not been able to reverse the declining trend, and its present condition and prospects, the former Congress President responded: “I am not so pessimistic. Consider that the Congress party and other opposition parties have not had a level playing field since this government came to power. Take into account the complete stranglehold they have on all institutions, especially the Election Commission, their control of mainstream media, their money power and their exploitation of religion. Yet, our party is fighting and making progress… What is more, it has been amply proved in recent months that many elections have been stolen, and people are now more aware of it. The Congress is working with like-minded parties, and our prospects are improving day by day.”
Sonia Gandhi’s much-awaited Belonging, published by HarperCollins India, is a personal memoir, with politics providing the background or “a kind of framework,” as she puts it in the book. I read it as a love story at its heart, the story of an extraordinary, instantly formed bond of love between Rajiv and Sonia, which gradually grew into something much larger, drawing her into his family, into the highest circles of power, then reluctantly into public life and politics, and eventually making her one of the country’s foremost political leaders.
“Stranger than fiction, isn’t it?” I asked her in the interview. “Yes!”, she responded. “That’s one reason I had no desire to talk about it for so long. But it is not only a love story between the two of us, it’s also the story of how I grew to love Rajiv’s family and the country to which they belonged, and then I too came to belong in it. And of how this love brought me into public life, when I saw the purpose of all the sacrifices they had made being threatened, and the party was weakening. I felt I had to do something.”
Rajiv Gandhi and Indira Gandhi, with whom she shared an exceptionally close bond, are the two central figures in Sonia’s story. Asked what, looking back, she saw as their defining qualities and how each shaped her life and outlook, she explained: “When I arrived in India as a young bride, I knew nothing about India. All that I am and know today, I learnt from them. Their courage, their empathy, their commitment to a secular and democratic India and most of all, the pull of duty that was greater than any other for both of them was something that inspired me and held me steadfast during times of difficulty and doubt.”
Asked how much of the young Italian woman who met Rajiv Gandhi at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge about sixty years ago survives in the Sonia of today, she replied: “The values that I learnt growing up survive ... But I used to smile and laugh a lot more then!”
She responded in some detail to questions about the Emergency of 1975-1977 as an anti-democratic and authoritarian chapter in the history of independent India; and the response needs to be read in its entirety to understand how she views the Emergency today.
In May 1999, when some party leaders, including Sharad Pawar, raised the issue of her foreign origin and asserted that she could not hold high office in India, she submitted her resignation as Congress President and then withdrew it. Asked about this, Sonia Gandhi responded, “Of course, I felt hurt…It came as a shock that they still saw me as an outsider.” But looking back, she could see “they may have had their own reasons.” She added that “after some soul-searching,” she realised that “I could not let my personal feelings divert me from my larger purpose. I had to continue.”
After the Congress-led victory in the 2004 Lok Sabha election, Sonia Gandhi, the obvious choice of the party and the coalition to become Prime Minister, declined the offer. But under intense pressure in “the surreal drama” that followed, she said “Theek hai," only to change her mind. Asked whether she had ever wondered how United Progressive Alliance policies and Congress strategy might have differed had she accepted, she replied emphatically: “No, not at all. That has never crossed my mind. Our experience was by and large a very positive one. We worked as a team, and our roles were distinct with him [Manmohan Singh] leading the government and I leading the party.”

briefs.headline: American national found dead in Gachibowli hotel room
briefs.deck: Lee, a resident of California, arrived in Hyderabad on November 2 along with his business partner, David Wu, for professional work. The two were staying at the hotel located at SLN Terminus
briefs.bodyText:
An American national, Mitchell Brian Lee, 41, was found dead in his hotel room at Marriott Executive Apartments in Gachibowli on Thursday (November 6, 2026) evening.
Lee, a resident of California, arrived in Hyderabad on November 2 along with his business partner, David Wu, for professional work. The two were staying at the hotel located at SLN Terminus.
According to police, Lee had not responded to phone calls since the evening of November 4. When there was no response, hotel staff opened the door to his room, number 1218 on the 12th floor, at around 6:30 p.m. on November 5 and found him lying unconscious on the bed.
The hotel staff alerted emergency services. A 108 ambulance team arrived at the scene and confirmed that he had died. Gachibowli police subsequently reached the hotel, inspected the room and initiated an investigation.
The cause of death is yet to be established. Police said it would be determined based on the post-mortem report and further investigation. All angles are being examined.

briefs.headline: China says discussions underway on Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
briefs.deck: President Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet President Xi for the third time this year, as the fragile trade truce is set to expire in January
briefs.bodyText:
Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China "is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state."
Nothing is set, but the three-leader gathering would take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in Shenzhen.
If it happens, it would be historic. Experts, however, say the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds, but they would gather for a photo, with China carefully choreographing the meeting.
"I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content," said Sun Yun, director of the China programme at the Stimson Center. "China wants the image but not the costs."
Beijing is the host of this year's leaders’ summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the U.S. and Russia.
President Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet President Xi for the third time this year, as the fragile trade truce is set to expire in January.
In a sign that tensions persist, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, in a Friday (November 6, 2026) video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, urged Beijing to take "concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals," according to a statement from Greer's office.
China's official news agency Xinhua reported Saturday (November 7) that both sides held in-depth, constructive exchanges on the call, and that China expressed concerns about Washington's restrictive economic and trade measures against Beijing.
While he's in China, Mr. Trump has said he would be interested in meeting Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin to discuss nuclear arms control, though Mr. Putin is focused on talking about the war in Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.
"President Putin has the most to gain from a leaders' trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup," said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former President Barack Obama's administration.
Mr. Trump, with his "crush on authoritarian strongmen", would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Sun of the Stimson Centre said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the U.S. closer to Moscow's positions on Ukraine, while "China will have to manage Russian manipulation".
China also would not engage in talks on arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace is important and wars should end, Sun said.
Beijing's biggest challenge may be the perception. The summit "should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world," she said.
The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Mr. Putin to be seen next to U.S. and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China programme at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
"But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns," Mr. Singleton said. "The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential."

briefs.headline: Telangana student goes missing in US, last seen leaving home for a walk
briefs.deck: Sreeja Reddy Koya, a 23-year-old student from Nalgonda, is missing in Boston after taking a walk. Local police report that she was last seen near her residence at about 9.45 pm on November 2. Friends became concerned and alerted authorities after she did not return. Her phone location pointed to an area close to the beach, but she remains unaccounted for.
briefs.bodyText:
HYDERABAD: A 23-year-old student from Nalgonda district, who is pursuing her master’s degree at the University of Massachusetts (UMass) in the US, has gone missing in Boston. According to local police, Sreeja Reddy Koya was last seen leaving her residence in Dorchester, near Edison Green, at around 9.45 pm on Nov 2 for an evening walk.
The incident came to light after her friends alerted the police when she failed to return from the walk. Her phone's location reportedly indicated an area near a beach, but her whereabouts remain unknown.
The Boston Police Department has issued a missing-person alert, seeking the public's assistance in tracing Sreeja. According to the alert, she may be in the vicinity of Carson Beach or Harbor Point.
“The Boston Police Department is actively working to locate Sreeja Koya and urges anyone with information regarding her whereabouts to call 911,” a notice on the department's website stated.
The University of Massachusetts has also made an appeal on social media, seeking information about its missing student.
According to the university’s notice, “Koya was seen wearing a black jacket, grey jeans and no shoes.” The notice further stated that she “may be experiencing a mental health crisis and is known to frequent the Carson Beach and Harbor Point areas”.
Sreeja is the daughter of Koya Yadagiri Reddy and Roopa, residents of Shabdullapuram village in Kanagal mandal of Nalgonda district. 
She moved to the US in 2025 to pursue a MS degree and is expected to complete the course in about six months, according to sources. Her parents are worried and anxiously awaiting information about their daughter’s whereabouts.
Local media reports said Sreeja had attended classes on the day she went missing, completed her part-time job and returned to her accommodation, which she shares with other Telugu students.
Roads and buildings minister Komatireddy Venkat Reddy has urged the Indian embassy, the ministry of external affairs (MEA), Boston police and other officials concerned to coordinate their efforts and ensure that Sreeja is traced safely. Meanwhile, Krishna Prasad of the Telugu Association of North America (TANA) said the organisation was coordinating with local officials, Sreeja’s friends and others to help trace her.

briefs.headline: Sonia Gandhi interview: ‘Great damage done to the fabric of India by BJP’
briefs.deck: Ahead of the launch of her book, Sonia Gandhi speaks to The Hindu, answering a number of questions — personal and political
briefs.bodyText:
In this wide-ranging interview to The Hindu on her soon-to-be-launched book, Belonging: A Journey of Love, published by HarperCollins India, Sonia Gandhi responds in writing to a number of questions, personal, historical, and political, raised by N. Ram.
The subjects covered include how she came to write her story about belonging; the values she grew up with and came to learn and cherish in India; what she learnt from Rajiv Gandhi and Indira Gandhi and how they shaped her life and outlook; the “great damage … done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions” by the BJP-RSS dispensation; how she viewed, and now looks back on, the Emergency of 1975-1977; the major political decisions she made to accept the office of Congress President in 1998 and to continue in it, after a challenge by some colleagues, in 1999, and in 2004 to decline the offer to become Prime Minister; the current political situation and the prospects of the Congress and its coalition partners; and the change of publisher in India just weeks before the book’s launch.
‘Others have spent decades telling my “story”,’ you posted on X the other day, ‘now it’s my turn.’ My AI-assisted bibliographical search suggests there are at least 75 books, including several biographies, that attempt or purport to tell your story in substantial measure. Your post hints that you were amused rather than irritated or angry about others presuming to tell your story. Am I right? And did you read those books, or at least some of them, written by biographers and others who spent decades telling your ‘story’?
I had no idea there were so many! But I have never felt like reading books about myself. A long time ago Rajiv and I realised that there was no point in trying to keep up with all that had been written about us. But, as I say in the book, there came a time when I felt that I should tell my own story.
In the Prologue to Belonging, you give us an insight into how you came to write your story, ‘perhaps…a story worth sharing,’ as you put it somewhat self-deprecatingly. Was it the ‘chorus’, which was on your case for years, or something within you, or both that eventually pushed you over the line to give us this intimate and unusually candid story? And may I ask how long it took you to write the book, breaks and all?
It’s been such a long time that I’ve lost track, but it has certainly been more than a decade since I first wrote a bit. I only started writing in earnest about five years ago. It wasn’t an uninterrupted process. There were times when words and thoughts flowed, others when nothing would come out, and I would throw my hands up in frustration.
You describe Belonging as a personal memoir, with politics providing the background or ‘a kind of framework’. But it’s really a love story at its heart and that’s how I read it. The story of an extraordinary, instantly formed magnetic bond of love between Rajiv and Sonia, which gradually grew into something much larger, drawing you into the highest circles of power, then reluctantly into public life and politics, and eventually making you one of the country’s foremost political leaders. Stranger than fiction, isn’t it?
Yes! That’s one reason I had no desire to talk about it for so long. But it is not only a love story between the two of us, it’s also the story of how I grew to love Rajiv’s family and the country to which they belonged, and then I too came to belong in it. And of how this love brought me into public life, when I saw the purpose of all the sacrifices they had made being threatened, and the party was weakening. I felt I had to do something.
The writer R.K. Narayan once observed that, despite the passage of time and physical ageing, ‘the chap inside is the same,’ capturing the enduring sense of self. You grew up in a small town in Italy, in a family and social environment far removed from the world that you would eventually inhabit and make your own. Looking back over more than six decades in India, how much of that young Italian woman survives in the person you are today?
The values that I learnt growing up survive. I have tried my best to be true to them: loyalty to family and friends, sincerity and feeling for others, the idea of being dutiful and responsible. I think I can say that in these I am the same person Rajiv met sixty years ago. But I used to smile and laugh a lot more then!
Also read | How a love story grew into a deep belonging to India
Rajiv Gandhi, the love of your life, and Indira Gandhi, with whom you shared an exceptionally close bond, are central figures in your story. Looking back, what do you see as their defining qualities and the ways in which each shaped your life and outlook?
When I arrived in India as a young bride, I knew nothing about India. All that I am and know today, I learnt from them. Their courage, their empathy, their commitment to a secular and democratic India and most of all, the pull of duty that was greater than any other for both of them was something that inspired me and held me steadfast during times of difficulty and doubt.
You write that Sanjay Gandhi’s name had become synonymous with the Emergency, and that Rajiv used to report complaints or feedback he had heard to his mother, but there was never any response from her. Do you think the so-called excesses of the Emergency could have been avoided had Indira Gandhi listened to her elder son and to others who were honest with her about what they had heard or experienced or observed?
It was not only Sanjay, though in the public mind he is often seen as synonymous with the Emergency. There was a lot of pressure from some of her senior colleagues, and I think there were very few people around her like Rajiv who had a different point of view. I think eventually my mother-in-law began to understand the situation through her own wisdom and took actions to remedy it.
The Emergency I lived through and opposed was, indisputably, a dark chapter in the history of independent India. Fortunately, it was short-lived for a complexity of reasons. You write interestingly about the Emergency in the book and it is clear that you disapprove, like Rajiv did, of many things that happened at that time. Would it not be correct to recognise it as an anti-democratic and authoritarian chapter rather than as a period of over-centralised governance marred by ‘excesses’?
It was only after the Emergency that I came to know the true gravity of what had been happening. Yes, democratic rights had been curtailed and there was a suspension of habeas corpus, but it was done constitutionally. Yet, when I take myself back to that period and try and see it from Mrs. Gandhi’s point of view, I see her struggling to cope with the rapidly deteriorating prevailing circumstances: violent protests, government offices and public transport set on fire, widespread organised unrest and even a call for the bureaucracy and armed forces to disobey orders. Hindsight allows us to put things better in perspective. Let’s not forget that it was Mrs. Gandhi herself who came to recognise what was happening and called for the March 1977 election. And you know very well that she herself later publicly expressed regret and apologised for excesses during the Emergency.
Some of the most interesting and insightful passages in your book concern the RSS, the BJP, and the Sangh Parivar, and the dangers they pose to India’s society and polity, particularly to the constitutional values of democracy, secularism, and fraternity. Do you think the Congress Party, historically and in recent times, has differentiated itself clearly, consistently, and effectively from the RSS-led Hindutva forces on these fundamental issues that matter so deeply to you?
But of course! I admit that there have been some within the party who felt we should not be so black and white on the issue of secularism. But that is not the Party view. In our policies and actions, I believe we have been steadfast in standing with the constitutional right of our people to worship and practise their religion and belief without fear.
On Prime Minister Narendra Modi, you write that you and he come from different ideological worlds and have very different ideas of India. Yet you also recognise something of his discomfort with the ruling elite. In a striking passage in the book, you recall feeling ill at ease in Delhi drawing rooms, where political opinions seemed ‘very far removed from the reality of India.’ The suffering and struggle to survive that you had witnessed in your constituency and across the country seemed unimaginable to this privileged group. You also observe that, although Modi’s humble origins may have been exaggerated by his PR team, he “had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world.” What political lessons should the Congress draw from this?
It’s true that he comes from a very different ideological world. But there are many ways that people succeed in politics – within the Congress party, take for example Dr. Manmohan Singh and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge. I don’t think we have much to learn from the RSS.
Also read | ‘Where I truly belong’: Sonia Gandhi on her memoir Belonging: A Journey of Love
You record your sense of hurt over Congress leaders Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma, and Tariq Anwar raising the issue of your foreign origin and asserting that you could not hold high office in India. ‘I felt tears welling up and walked out of the meeting. I hadn’t entered politics to grab position and power. It was some of these colleagues who had urged me to join politics, and now they were turning on me…It wasn’t the issue of holding office that hurt me; it was that my loyalty to India was being questioned.’ You submitted your resignation as Congress President, but you were persuaded by party leaders to continue. Did this episode steel your resolve not to accept the prime ministership should the opportunity arise?
Of course, I felt hurt. These were my colleagues and they’d had my trust, but then it turned out that I didn’t have theirs. It came as a shock that they still saw me as an outsider. Looking back, I can see they may have had their own reasons. But this was early in my political life, and the idea of prime ministership couldn’t have been further from my mind. Yes, I did resign, but then after some soul-searching I realised that I could not let my personal feelings divert me from my larger purpose. I had to continue.
Chapter Thirty is, arguably, the most interesting chapter politically, and one of the most moving personally. It offers new insights into your decision not to become Prime Minister after the Congress-led victory in 2004, when virtually everyone expected you to take office. Months before the general election, you had told one of your children, “Absolutely not,” when asked whether you would accept the post should the Congress pull off a win. Rahul and Priyanka were strongly opposed, haunted by the assassinations of their grandmother and father and convinced that the office carried exceptional danger. Yet, amid the ‘surreal drama’ of party leaders pressing you to accept, you relented with a ‘Theek hai’, only to change your mind. Dr. Manmohan Singh became Prime Minister instead. Do you ever wonder how UPA policies and Congress strategy might have differed had you accepted? I ask because you are widely seen as more of a social democrat than Dr. Singh and most Congress leaders, then and now.
No, not at all. That has never crossed my mind. Our experience was by and large a very positive one. We worked as a team, and our roles were distinct with him leading the government and I leading the party.
You make it clear in the Epilogue that you have no regrets in your personal life over coming to India and making your life here with the family you married into. You also strike a hopeful note when you observe that when you joined the Congress Party and became its President, you discovered that ‘individuals have untapped reserves that come into play when life calls them to perform tasks they had thought unimaginable.’ However, you write that where you struggled with doubts was when you were called upon to make political compromises. ‘I ask myself now,’ you write, ‘did those compromises even serve their objectives? Not always. Even when they seemed to favour the party, I couldn’t rejoice, deep down. They still don’t sit lightly on my conscience.’ What were these compromises? Could you give us a couple of examples?
Let’s be realistic, in politics compromises are at times unavoidable. Sometimes we were faced with difficult political choices, when we were obliged to join hands with some who did not share our political ideology. It never sat easy in my mind. But of one thing I am perfectly clear: we never made any compromises with the BJP and the RSS and we never will.
You rue the end of decency and decorum in parliamentary politics and public life in the last decade and more – ‘a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes to belittle and torment those who differ from them.’ Do you believe things will change and politics will return to a contest over policies and programmes if the BJP is voted out of power in the 2029 Lok Sabha election?
Over the last twelve years great damage has been done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions. Even after this government goes it will take time to restore our systems back to health, and great effort from political parties. People are now beginning to be restless and recognising the damage. But I am optimistic and I know that the people of India will welcome a return to proper governance.
The decline of the Congress as India’s dominant party is a fact of political life. Over the past three decades, the Congress has struggled to halt the advances made by the Hindutva forces. There was some revival of fortunes between 2004 and 2014, but critics say that the party has not been able to reverse the declining trend. You write extensively about the Congress in your book. How do you assess its present condition and prospects?
I am not so pessimistic. Consider that the Congress party and other opposition parties have not had a level playing field since this government came to power. Take into account the complete stranglehold they have on all institutions, especially the Election Commission, their control of mainstream media, their money power and their exploitation of religion. Yet, our party is fighting and making progress, in fact, it is the only party that has had the resilience to withstand this onslaught. Our workers and leaders have been extremely courageous. They have faced persecution of all kinds and yet, in every village and every district, congressmen and women are still fighting for the values enshrined in our Constitution. What is more, it has been amply proved in recent months that many elections have been stolen, and people are now more aware of it. The Congress is working with like-minded parties, and our prospects are improving day by day.
It is unusual for a book of such personal and political significance, certain to attract a wide readership in India and abroad, to change publishers just months before its launch. In late August 2026, it emerged that Penguin Random House India would no longer publish Belonging: A Journey of Love. In early September, HarperCollins India announced its publication on November 10. The change prompted considerable speculation. One newspaper report suggested disagreements over passages concerning Narendra Modi, the RSS, communal tensions and minorities, and India’s confrontation with China, including Galwan. Penguin said that following disagreements over the manuscript your team decided not to proceed with publication. Is that account correct? Was this a disagreement over the book’s contents, or were larger questions of a writer’s freedom of expression involved?
I would rather not involve myself in these controversies.

stories.headline: Bengaluru developers get more room to use premium FAR as Karnataka raises high-rise threshold from 21m to 24m, allowing buildings with 7-8 floors to fall below the revised limit
stories.deck: Karnataka is raising the bar for fire safety by redefining high-rise buildings. Now, structures with 7-8 floors will be considered high-rises, up from the earlier norm. This shift not only benefits builders by maximizing premium floor area ratios but also emphasizes the importance of ongoing fire safety reviews for critical infrastructures like schools and hospitals. The government aims to…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: In line with the Centre's push for achieving global standards on fire safety, Karnataka govt issued an order early this week changing the definition of a highrise from 21 to 24 metres. This effectively means buildings with 7-8 floors will qualify as high-rise structures as opposed to the earlier threshold of 6-7 floors.
The urban development department, in its notification, said the new definition follows the Centre's recommendations on regulatory requirements and the adoption of global best practices in building fire safety.
Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda said height relaxation will go a long way in facilitating ease-of-doing business.
Sources said the larger objective was to help builders who were unable to use the premium floor area ratio (FAR) being sold to developers. "The govt was issuing premium FARs but there was no space to utilise the same. This will help in better utilisation of the available FAR," said past president of Credai Suresh Hari, adding in other places builders and developers were unable to use the space even with the available setbacks.
Costwise, too, it will help in spreading out the area where the FAR is being utilised, Hari said, calling it a positive decision. Credai, or Confederation of Real Estate Developers' Associations of India, is an apex body for private real estate developers.
Gowda said that it's a move to reduce compliance burden and enhance ease of governance, rationalisation and adoption of global best practices in fire safety norms for buildings.
Min: Outdated rules are being re-evaluated Rigid and outdated requirements are being re-evaluated, he said, adding central govt had even identified fire certificate renewal as a recurring administrative burden. "Without considering specific building risks, imposing uniform requirements irrespective of actual risk profiles leads to repeated costs and additional documentation for applicants," he said.
Byre Gowda said high-risk category buildings such as industries, schools and hospitals are approved based on fire-safety evaluation.
The state fire and emergency services department opined that height reference for highrises may be increased, subject to its adoption in the applicable zonal regulations.

stories.headline: E20 or E31? Karnataka lab tests show ‘excess’ ethanol
stories.deck: Lab tests conducted across Karnataka discovered that several petrol stations exceeded the allowed ethanol blend in petrol. The blending levels found at some stations reached up to 31.2%, far above the 20% limit. This excessive mixing could result in a significant drop in fuel mileage, affecting consumers financially. The Karnataka government has demanded clearer regulations on ethanol blending…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Karnataka govt-authorised lab tests of E20 blend have found “excess” mixing of ethanol by more than 10% per litre of petrol in several samples.
On Friday, state food and civil supplies and legal metrology minister Rizwan Arshad shared the results for samples collected from 63 petrol bunks across Karnataka.
The samples included fuel from IOCL, HPCL, BPCL, Nayara, Shell and MRPL facilities. Tests of samples from 14 of the bunks found ethanol levels above the prescribed limit.
The results revealed ethanol blending of 31.2% and 30.5% at some IOCL and HPCL petrol bunks, respectively, which were way beyond the stipulated 20%. Blending at some BPCL, Nayara, and Shell bunks was also found to be beyond the prescribed limit.
The minister claimed that an estimated 10% drop in mileage due to ethanol blending would cost consumers as much as Rs 62,000 crore, based on petrol sales of 6,200 crore litres between April 2025 and April 2026 at Rs 100-110 per litre.
Arshad said under the directives of chief minister DK Shivakumar, his department conducted the inspections across Karnataka. “The results have raised serious concerns over transparency, regulatory compliance, and consumers’ right to know what goes in the fuel [they’re using],” Arshad added.
He further clarified that neither he nor Karnataka govt was against blending of ethanol in petrol. “However, I am against the handling of the entire issue by central govt and the way people are being penalised,” he added.
In its recommendation, Karnataka govt demanded that the Centre publicly clarify the “actual ethanol blend” being supplied to consumers, and penalties be imposed on all OMCs supplying petrol above 20% ethanol blend. It has also pressed for E20 spoilage fund to compensate every consumer for the loss incurred.
The state govt has sought mandatory blend displays at fuel pumps across the nation to allow consumers to choose between the range of blends available.
OMCs question sampling and testing methods
IOCL, BPCL and HPCL said Friday E20 petrol supplied by them across India, including in Karnataka, conforms to the Bureau of Indian Standards specification. The three public sector Oil Marketing Companies also raised concerns about the sampling procedure and methodology adopted for the tests.
They said the Oct samples were collected without OMC representatives and that the companies had not received outlet-wise reports, retention samples or details needed to verify the results. They also questioned whether the third-party lab used the prescribed testing method.

stories.headline: Karnataka CM ridicules BJP leaders for trying to take credit for PM’s visit
stories.bodyText:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar on Friday alleged that some BJP leaders were trying to take credit for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Bengaluru on November 13 to inaugurate the metro Pink Line, even though he was arriving on the official invitation of the State government.
Without taking the name of BJP MP Tejasvi Surya, the Chief Minister alleged that some BJP leaders were trying to take publicity by claiming that they were responsible for the Prime Minsiter’s proposed visit.
Speaking to media persons in Kanakapura, he wondered why the BJP leaders were tying to take publicity for this event though they had nothing to do with it.
“We are developing metro network by borrowing money. I will present some of these issues before the Prime Minister on November 13,” he said.

stories.headline: Bengaluru: Seven-murder accused allegedly terrorised neighbours for years, say residents
stories.deck: Anand E., president of a small political party that operates from a small space on the first floor, just below Indushekhar’s house, said he had been threatened by him.
stories.bodyText:
“It’s just another face of him.” This is how residents of the neighbourhood near Bhashyam Circle in Rajajinagar described Indushekhar, the man accused of murdering seven family members. In fact, the area seemed to have heaved a sigh of relief following his arrest. It has now come to light that Indushekar also had a chain-snatching case registered against him at the Madanayakanahalli police station.
Venkatesh, a nearby stove repairer, said, “Many residents have vacated the place, unable to bear the torture inflicted by Indushekhar. He was a nightmare in the colony.”
Anand E., president of a small political party that operates from a small space on the first floor, just below Indushekhar’s house, said he had been threatened by him.
“When we moved into this space, our landlord asked us not to engage in conversations with Indushekhar, and we refrained from doing so. Once, when we held a meeting inside our makeshift office, he came, recorded videos and even threatened to expose us, although we were not doing anything wrong,” he said. Residents said Indushekhar used his YouTube channel, ‘Taana Varadi’, and his monthly tabloid as weapons.
A worker at Shankar Watches, located on the ground floor, told The Hindu that Indushekhar had been living in the building for over 15 years and was friends with the landlord’s son.
“Despite that, he filed a civil case claiming that the house where he was staying belonged to him. We are unsure how he managed to do that, but the case is ongoing, and in the meantime, the landlord died,” he said.
That was not all. He said Indushekhar would pick frequent quarrels with motorists over parking on the road where the building stands.

briefs.headline: More skeletons tumble out in Bengaluru family massacre: TV at full blast, property dispute, 20-year conflict with wife
briefs.deck: S Indushekhar, a 52-year-old cab driver, is suspected of murdering his wife and six relatives. The victims were reportedly invited to his home for meals before their deaths occurred. Indushekhar was arrested while a minor boy, his eighth target, was found in his vehicle. The accused allegedly used a grindstone to commit these murders during late October.
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: In a series of grisly murders committed over a 15-day period in late Oct, a 52-year-old cab driver allegedly killed his wife and six members of her extended family and dumped their bodies at four locations in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. His wife, mother-in-law and seven-year-old nephew were among the victims, police said.
Police identified the accused as S Indushekhar alias Arjun Indushekhar, who lived in Rajajinagar’s V Block. When he was arrested near Ulsoorgate on Wednesday, a minor boy — said to be his eighth target — was found in his car. “Indushekhar claimed he had planned to kill the boy as well,” a police officer said, adding the accused is being interrogated in police custody.
His daughter, 17, is suspected to have helped him in committing multiple murders.
Police alleged the accused invited the victims to his second-floor house between Oct 16 and 31 for lunch or dinner, and crushed them to death with a grindstone. During questioning, Indushekhar allegedly told investigators he had been ‘in conflict with’ his wife for nearly 20 years and blamed the relatives for supporting her during their disputes.
Cops yet to recover 7 
The victims were identified as his wife Sunita (40); mother-in-law Rupavathi (65); brother-in-law Shivakumar (46); his wife Divya (30); brother-in-law Shankar (44); his wife Nalini (29); and their son Puneeth (7). Police commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh called the incident “serious” and added that the motive appears to be personal. The case came to light after relatives of the missing persons failed to establish contact with them and sought help from police to find their whereabouts.
Thunganamma approached Srirampura police on Nov 3 to report that her daughter Nalini, Shankar and several relatives were missing, and their phones remained switched off on Oct 31 and Nov 1.
Kalavathi similarly separately reported to police about her daughter Divya, son-in-law Shivakumar and grandson Puneeth.

briefs.headline: Karnataka milk price hike justified by rising cost of production: D.K. Suresh
briefs.deck: After the latest round of price revision, the farmers are receiving ₹42 as the procurement price per litre, while they also get ₹5 per litre as an incentive
briefs.bodyText:
Defending the recent hike in the price of milk and curd by the Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF), the president of Bengaluru Milk Union Ltd., D.K. Suresh, said that if the hike had not been implemented, there were fears of dairy farmers giving up owing to meagre earnings.
Despite the hike in the price of milk in the range of ₹8 to ₹12 per litre and curd by ₹14 a kg, the price of milk was still lower in Karnataka compared to the prevailing price in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (₹66 a litre), Gujarat (₹57 a litre) and Uttar Pradesh (₹59 a litre), Mr. Suresh told The Hindu on Friday.
“Farmers had been demanding an upward revision of the procurement price for the last six months. The cost of oil cake has increased by up to 80%, while the cost of bran, maize and cattle feed has increased by 49%. The price of maize per tonne has increased from ₹22,000 to ₹35,000 a tonne. The cost of soya cake has increased from ₹35,000 to ₹64,000 a tonne. There is a severe shortage of green fodder. Farmers would have moved away from dairy farming if the procurement price had not been increased,” he said, defending the hike. The Bangalore Urban, Rural and Ramanagara District Co-operative Milk Producers’ Societies Union Ltd. (Bamul) president also said that farmers could start selling milk to private milk dairies that pay them ₹42 per litre.
After the latest round of price revision, the farmers are receiving ₹42 per litre as the procurement price, while they also get ₹5 per litre as an incentive.
Mr. Suresh claimed that the KMF had witnessed an increase in the procurement of milk by about 10 lakh litres after the increase in the procurement price. On average, the KMF is now procuring 1.16 crore litres a day. “Unemployment and migration have also declined as young people are buying one or two cows and selling milk to the KMF. The government incentive of ₹5 per litre is also encouraging dairy farmers. The government spends about ₹2,500 crores annually.”
Elaborating on the cost of producing milk for the district unions, he said that the cost of plastic crates, culture used in curd, fat used in milk, furnace oil, commercial diesel and gas, refrigeration and electricity had all gone up since the war began in West Asia, besides the cost of ESI and Provident Fund. “The cost of furnace oil has gone up by 40%; commercial diesel costs ₹115 a litre, a commercial gas cylinder is ₹600, and the cost of a crate has gone from ₹250 to ₹360. The overall production cost has increased by at least 40%,” he said.
Prices of curd to be reduced post deepavali
Bamul president D.K. Suresh said that a slight downward revision in curd prices is expected post Deepavali. “We have to follow the instructions of the government to reduce the price of curd. It will be reduced after Deepavali, after holding a meeting with the presidents of milk unions across the State. Revised prices will be released soon,” he said. The price of one litre of curd is ₹68 per litre now.
